paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend. The best plan in the room still loses when the LORD has other plans. Ahithophel's advice was so trusted that it was treated "like the consultation of the word of God" (2 Samuel 16:23), and the passage says his counsel was good. Yet "the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom" (2 Samuel 17:14). Smart, strong and popular does not beat God. Not even close.

Now look at who God used. A friend who stood in the enemy's office and gave a speech, two messengers hiding in a well, and a woman with a covering and some grain. Nobody in that list was a king, and every one of them had a small job to do. God's purposes run through ordinary people doing the part in front of them. I spent years in a junk drawer, so trust me, I know small doesn't mean unused.

And then there's the heavy ending. Ahithophel saw his advice ignored, and his story stops in a very sad place (2 Samuel 17:23). I think that's the part to sit with, friend. It shows how far a person can fall when their whole confidence is in their own plans, so keep yours in the LORD. This story isn't over yet, so keep your oven warm.
